extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy/natural philosophy (philosophers, advanced students of metaphysics and philosophy of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for constructing a comprehensive philosophical theory that unifies scientific explanations into a universal account of change (integration/evolution and diffusion/dissolution), specifying laws, conditions, and the role of matter and motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal synthesis (philosophical goal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate interpretation to be reached by Philosophy is a universal synthesis comprehending and consolidating such special syntheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical truths alone (even a number of them) cannot constitute the synthesis of thought which interprets the synthesis of things. Philosophy must unify the various scientific syntheses (e.g., chemistry, geology, biology) into a coherent whole that reveals common elements across concrete processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of composition of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek a law of composition of phenomena, co-extensive with the laws of their components, that specifies how the joint action of factors produces complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having ascertained the laws of factors (matter, motion, force), the chief problem is to show how their joint action results in phenomena in all their complexity. The sought law must specify the combined consequences of separately formulated actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify changes of both matter and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory formula must specify the course of the changes undergone by both matter and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every transformation implies re-arrangement of component parts and changes in the movements (sensible or insensible). A definition must say what happens to both sensible/insensible portions of substance and to the concomitant motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify conditions for commencement, cessation, reversal
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula must specify the conditions under which a transformation commences, ceases, and is reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless transformations always proceed in the same way and at the same rate, the law must indicate the initiating and terminating conditions and what reverses the process — i.e., boundary/conditional clauses for dynamic processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of continuous redistribution of matter and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The general law to be sought is the law of the continuous redistribution of matter and motion; absolute rest and permanence do not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every object undergoes instant-to-instant alteration of state via gains or losses of motion and changes in parts' relations. The dynamic principle should express these ever-changing relations both in detail and as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include past and future (evolution and dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire history must include appearance out of the imperceptible and disappearance into the imperceptible; philosophy must formulate passage from imperceptible to perceptible and back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge is incomplete unless it unites past, present, and future histories of objects. The general law of redistribution must also unify successive changes that sensible existences pass through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose opposite processes: concentration (integration) and diffusion (disintegration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula must comprehend the two opposite processes of concentration (integration) and diffusion (disintegration), i.e., change from diffused to concentrated states and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change to a concentrated, perceptible state is integration of matter with dissipation of motion; change to a diffused, imperceptible state is absorption of motion with concomitant disintegration. Constituent parts aggregating lose relative motion; separation gains relative motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between internal motion and degree of integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A progressing consolidation involves a decrease of internal motion; increase of internal motion involves progressing unconsolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal (molecular/thermal) motion determines facility of rearrangement: aggregates with large internal motion allow secondary redistributions and complex evolution; low internal motion limits secondary rearrangements and yields simpler evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal dichotomy: every change is toward integration or disintegration
rubrics_metrics.description: Every change undergone by every sensible existence is a change in one or other of the two opposite directions: towards greater concentration (integration) or towards greater diffusion (disintegration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claim applies across additions/subtractions of matter, thermal expansion/contraction, and transpositions; any internal redistribution altering average distances of parts counts as advancing integration or disintegration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish simple and compound evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where forces producing aggregation/diffusion dominate, evolution is simple; when integration is slow and other forces produce appreciable secondary rearrangements, evolution is compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compound evolution arises when retained internal motion, large aggregate size, or external inputs permit significant secondary redistributions during primary integration. The theory must explain when and why simple vs compound evolution occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for role of incident/perturbing forces vs cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how incident forces produce equivalent changes when parts are free but are dissipated (producing other changes) when parts are bound by cohesion or gravitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In loosely aggregated systems, incident forces effect marked re-arrangements; in strongly bound systems, small perturbations mainly modify insensible molecular motions. The effect accumulates with time and depends on degree of binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal accumulation and facilitation of secondary redistributions
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of secondary redistribution accompanying primary integration is proportional to the quantity of internal motion retained and to the time that internal motion is retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether internal motion persists because of material properties, aggregate size, or external supply, retained motion makes secondary re-distributions facile and their accumulation possible. Conversely, rapid loss of motion limits such secondary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical exemplification: agitation, heat, and material treatment as mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use empirical cases (shaking a vessel of fragments, tempering steel, annealing glass, cloud condensation) to illustrate how agitation or heat facilitates rearrangement and segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate the general principle that adding sensible or insensible motion (vibration, heat) enables forces to re-arrange components (settling, segregation by density, crystallization, annealing). These serve as methodological analogies for theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definitions of key terms (evolution, dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explicit definitions: Evolution = integration of matter with concomitant dissipation of motion; Dissolution = absorption of motion with concomitant disintegration of matter (with caveats about ordinary language usage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ordinary meanings of 'evolution' can conflict with this technical sense, the theory must clearly define terms and note possible confusions (e.g., gas evolution being opposite in ordinary usage).
